questions.stem: Which structural characteristic distinguishes purine bases from pyrimidines?
questions.why: Purines have fused six- and five-membered nitrogen-containing rings, unlike single-ring pyrimidines.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a nucleotide from its corresponding nucleoside?
questions.why: A nucleoside contains base and sugar; addition of one or more phosphate groups produces a nucleotide.

questions.stem: Removal of phosphate from guanosine monophosphate yields which product?
questions.why: Dephosphorylation of GMP produces the nucleoside guanosine.

questions.stem: Which pathway supplies ribose-5-phosphate for de novo purine synthesis?
questions.why: The pentose phosphate pathway supplies ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme produces PRPP from ribose-5-phosphate and ATP?
questions.why: PRPP synthetase activates ribose-5-phosphate to phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate.

questions.stem: Which compound is the substrate of the first committed purine biosynthetic reaction?
questions.why: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase converts PRPP to 5-phosphoribosylamine.

questions.stem: Which amino acid donates the nitrogen in the committed step of purine synthesis?
questions.why: Glutamine donates its amide nitrogen as PRPP is converted to phosphoribosylamine.

questions.stem: What product is formed immediately by glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase?
questions.why: The committed reaction replaces the pyrophosphate of PRPP with a nitrogen from glutamine.

questions.stem: Which purine-ring position receives nitrogen from the first committed glutamine reaction?
questions.why: The first glutamine amide nitrogen becomes purine N9.

questions.stem: Which amino acid contributes two carbons and one nitrogen to the purine ring?
questions.why: Glycine supplies C4, C5 and N7 during purine-ring assembly.

questions.stem: Which cofactor contributes two formyl groups during assembly of the purine ring?
questions.why: Two one-carbon units enter purine synthesis through N10-formyltetrahydrofolate.

questions.stem: Which two amino acids provide nitrogen without providing a carbon atom to the purine ring?
questions.why: Glutamine supplies N3 and N9 while aspartate supplies N1; glycine also contributes carbon.

questions.stem: Which nucleotide is the first completed purine product of de novo synthesis?
questions.why: IMP is the first full purine nucleotide, and its base is hypoxanthine.

questions.stem: Which nucleotide provides energy during conversion of IMP to AMP?
questions.why: Adenylosuccinate synthetase uses GTP to add aspartate to IMP en route to AMP.

questions.stem: Which intermediate lies between IMP and GMP during de novo synthesis?
questions.why: IMP dehydrogenase converts IMP to XMP, which is converted to GMP.

questions.stem: A drug blocks IMP dehydrogenase. Production of which nucleotide is most directly reduced?
questions.why: IMP dehydrogenase forms XMP in the GMP branch; blocking it reduces guanine nucleotide synthesis.

questions.stem: Why does AMP synthesis require GTP but GMP synthesis require ATP?

options.label: D
options.text: To bypass the common IMP intermediate

options.label: E
options.text: To prevent salvage of both bases

questions.why: Cross-use of energy nucleotides helps maintain balanced AMP and GMP formation.

questions.stem: High cellular AMP most directly inhibits which enzyme in its synthesis branch?
questions.why: AMP feedback inhibits adenylosuccinate synthetase, reducing further AMP synthesis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is directly feedback-inhibited by GMP at the IMP branch point?
questions.why: GMP inhibits the enzyme that converts IMP to XMP in the guanine nucleotide pathway.

questions.stem: Excess AMP and GMP jointly slow the committed de novo purine reaction through which enzyme?
questions.why: AMP and GMP exert cumulative feedback inhibition of purine amidotransferase.

questions.stem: Why may an increased PRPP supply accelerate de novo purine synthesis?

options.label: E
options.text: It prevents ribose synthesis in the cell

questions.why: Elevated PRPP can stimulate the committed amidotransferase step despite end-product feedback.

questions.stem: Azaserine inhibits the purine committed step because it resembles which amino acid?
questions.why: Azaserine is a glutamine analogue that interferes with glutamine amidotransferase reactions.

questions.stem: What is released when HGPRT uses PRPP to salvage a purine base?
questions.why: Purine phosphoribosyltransferases transfer ribose phosphate from PRPP and release pyrophosphate.

questions.stem: Which tissues are emphasized in the lecture as strongly relying on purine salvage?
questions.why: The lecture emphasizes brain and leucocytes as relying strongly on recycling purine bases rather than de novo synthesis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme uses PRPP to recover free adenine as AMP?
questions.why: APRT salvages adenine by attaching ribose phosphate from PRPP.

questions.stem: Why does purine salvage consume less energy than de novo synthesis?

options.label: B
options.text: It synthesizes every ring carbon afresh

options.label: E
options.text: It diverts all nitrogen to the urea cycle

questions.why: Salvage uses existing purine bases rather than rebuilding purine rings.

questions.stem: Which product forms when adenosine deaminase acts on adenosine?
questions.why: Adenosine deaminase removes an amino group to form inosine.

questions.stem: Inosine is converted to hypoxanthine by which enzyme?
questions.why: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase generates hypoxanthine and ribose-1-phosphate.

questions.stem: Guanine must first be converted to which base to enter the final urate pathway?
questions.why: Guanine deaminase converts guanine to xanthine.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly represents late hypoxanthine degradation?
questions.why: Xanthine oxidase sequentially oxidizes hypoxanthine to xanthine and then to uric acid.

questions.stem: Nucleoside phosphorylase generates which sugar product during nucleoside breakdown?
questions.why: Phosphorolysis of nucleosides generates ribose-1-phosphate and a free base.

questions.stem: Conversion of muscle IMP back to AMP during exertion consumes which combination?
questions.why: The purine nucleotide cycle uses GTP and aspartate during adenylosuccinate formation.

questions.stem: Which TCA-cycle intermediate emerges from adenylosuccinate cleavage in muscle?
questions.why: Adenylosuccinate lyase releases fumarate during AMP regeneration.

questions.stem: Which enzyme catalyses AMP plus ATP converting to two ADP?
questions.why: Adenylate kinase interconverts adenine nucleotide phosphorylation states.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts many nucleoside diphosphates to triphosphates regardless of their bases?
questions.why: NDP kinase exchanges phosphate groups without strict base specificity.

questions.stem: What structural difference distinguishes de novo pyrimidine-ring assembly from purine assembly?

options.label: B
options.text: Pyrimidine ring grows directly on PRPP

options.label: C
options.text: Purine ring is first built as a free base

options.label: D
options.text: Pyrimidine ring forms only after UMP

options.label: E
options.text: Purine ring forms only after nucleosides

questions.why: Pyrimidine rings are made before attachment to ribose phosphate; purine rings are built on PRPP.

questions.stem: Which enzyme forms carbamoyl phosphate for mammalian pyrimidine synthesis?
questions.why: Cytosolic CPS II starts pyrimidine synthesis using glutamine and bicarbonate.

questions.stem: A mitochondrial CPS I defect most directly compromises which process?

options.label: C
options.text: Entry of ammonia into the urea cycle

questions.why: CPS I functions in the urea cycle, while cytosolic CPS II functions in pyrimidine synthesis.

questions.stem: What enzyme condenses carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate in pyrimidine synthesis?
questions.why: Aspartate transcarbamoylase produces carbamoyl aspartate.

questions.stem: Which enzyme cyclizes carbamoyl aspartate to dihydroorotate?
questions.why: Dihydroorotase closes the pyrimidine ring.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Mammalian dihydroorotate oxidation is the mitochondrial step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis.
Reason: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase transfers electrons to ubiquinone in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.why: The mitochondrion-associated dihydroorotate dehydrogenase transfers electrons to ubiquinone, explaining the location.

questions.stem: How many ATP molecules are consumed when mammalian CPS II forms carbamoyl phosphate?
questions.why: CPS II consumes two ATP molecules to make carbamoyl phosphate.

questions.stem: Which donor attaches an activated ribose phosphate to orotate?
questions.why: Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase forms OMP using PRPP.

questions.stem: Which enzyme generates UMP by removing carbon dioxide from OMP?
questions.why: OMP decarboxylase produces UMP in the final step of pyrimidine de novo synthesis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme directly converts UTP to CTP in an ATP-dependent reaction?
questions.why: CTP synthetase transfers glutamine-derived nitrogen to UTP.

questions.stem: Which amino acid donates nitrogen for conversion of UTP to CTP?
questions.why: CTP synthetase uses the amide nitrogen of glutamine.

questions.stem: Which nitrogen source is used by CPS II but not by urea-cycle CPS I?
questions.why: Cytosolic CPS II uses glutamine amide nitrogen; mitochondrial CPS I uses free ammonia.

questions.stem: Which metabolite allosterically inhibits mammalian CPS II at high concentration?
questions.why: UTP provides feedback inhibition of mammalian CPS II, limiting further pyrimidine synthesis.

questions.stem: Which metabolite is an allosteric activator of mammalian CPS II?
questions.why: PRPP activates CPS II and promotes pyrimidine synthesis when activated ribose is available.

questions.stem: An E. coli cell accumulates CTP. Which biosynthetic enzyme is most directly feedback inhibited?
questions.why: Bacterial ATCase responds to CTP feedback, unlike mammalian regulation primarily at CPS II.

questions.stem: Why does ATP activate bacterial aspartate transcarbamoylase?

options.label: A
options.text: To balance purine and pyrimidine production

options.label: B
options.text: To inhibit glutamine formation in the liver

options.label: C
options.text: To suppress formation of all nucleotides

options.label: D
options.text: To favor degradation of available pyrimidines

questions.why: ATP activation of bacterial ATCase coordinates pyrimidine synthesis with the cellular purine and energy supply.

questions.stem: Which multifunctional complex catalyses the first three steps of mammalian pyrimidine synthesis?
questions.why: CAD contains carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, aspartate transcarbamoylase and dihydroorotase activities.

questions.stem: Why can linking the first three pyrimidine enzymes into CAD increase efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Intermediates are hydrolysed in extracellular fluid

options.label: B
options.text: ATP is no longer needed for any reaction

options.label: C
options.text: Intermediates are passed directly between sites

options.label: E
options.text: Enzymes no longer require their substrates

questions.why: Substrate channeling can protect intermediates and speed multistep catalysis.

questions.stem: Which atoms of the pyrimidine ring are contributed by aspartate?
questions.why: Aspartate contributes N1 and C4–C6; bicarbonate provides C2 and glutamine contributes N3.

questions.stem: Which atom of the pyrimidine ring derives from bicarbonate?
questions.why: Bicarbonate contributes the C2 carbon of the pyrimidine ring.

questions.stem: Which bifunctional protein catalyses the final two steps from orotate to UMP?
questions.why: UMP synthase combines the orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase activities.

questions.stem: Which cofactor requirement distinguishes the OMP decarboxylase reaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Biotin is needed for carbon transfer

options.label: C
options.text: PLP is needed for amino transfer

options.label: E
options.text: FAD is needed for electron transfer

questions.why: OMP decarboxylase catalyses rapid decarboxylation without an added cofactor.

questions.stem: How can administered uridine improve nucleotide supply in hereditary orotic aciduria?

options.label: A
options.text: It directly restores the mutant UMP synthase

options.label: C
options.text: It bypasses the defective de novo steps

options.label: E
options.text: It converts excess orotate into purines

questions.why: Uridine enters salvage routes to produce UMP downstream of the defective OMP-forming steps.

questions.stem: A child has megaloblastic anaemia with urinary orotate but no hyperammonaemia. What best explains the pattern?

options.label: C
options.text: Primary defect of hepatic CPS I

questions.why: UMP synthase deficiency causes hereditary orotic aciduria with impaired pyrimidine availability; OTC deficiency usually causes hyperammonaemia.

questions.stem: What major product arises from degradation of the pyrimidine base uracil?
questions.why: Uracil breakdown yields beta-alanine along with carbon dioxide and ammonia.

questions.stem: Which pyrimidine base produces beta-aminoisobutyrate during its breakdown?
questions.why: Thymine is degraded to beta-aminoisobutyrate; uracil instead yields beta-alanine.

questions.stem: Which process chiefly distinguishes pyrimidine degradation from purine degradation in humans?

options.label: A
options.text: Formation of uric acid as the final product

options.label: B
options.text: Ring reduction rather than terminal urate formation

options.label: C
options.text: Transfer of glycine to an intact purine ring

options.label: D
options.text: Complete salvage of all bases before breakdown

options.label: E
options.text: Oxidation of bases exclusively by xanthine oxidase

questions.why: Pyrimidine bases undergo reduction and ring opening; purines commonly end as uric acid.

questions.stem: Which enzyme starts reductive degradation of uracil to dihydrouracil?
questions.why: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase reduces uracil during pyrimidine catabolism.

questions.stem: Beta-alanine generated during uracil degradation can contribute to synthesis of which compound?
questions.why: The nucleotide metabolism slide identifies beta-alanine as a contributor to coenzyme A formation.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ribonucleotide reductase produces deoxyribonucleotides for DNA synthesis.
Reason: It removes the 2-prime hydroxyl from a ribonucleoside diphosphate.
questions.why: Ribonucleotide reductase reduces the ribose 2-prime position of NDPs to generate deoxy-NDPs for DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: Which characteristic mechanism is used by ribonucleotide reductase during nucleotide reduction?
questions.why: Ribonucleotide reductase uses a radical-based catalytic mechanism.

questions.stem: Which reducing system supplies electrons needed by ribonucleotide reductase?
questions.why: Thioredoxin and glutaredoxin transfer reducing equivalents to ribonucleotide reductase.

questions.stem: What part of ribose is chemically changed by ribonucleotide reductase?

options.label: A
options.text: The phosphate group at carbon 5 prime

options.label: B
options.text: The nitrogenous base at carbon 1 prime

options.label: C
options.text: The hydroxyl group at carbon 2 prime

options.label: D
options.text: The carbonyl group at carbon 3 prime

questions.why: Ribonucleotide reductase removes the 2-prime hydroxyl to generate the deoxyribose moiety needed for DNA.

questions.stem: Mycophenolic acid reduces guanine nucleotide synthesis mainly by inhibiting which enzyme?
questions.why: IMP dehydrogenase converts IMP to XMP and is inhibited by mycophenolic acid.

questions.stem: Which class of metabolic reaction is inhibited by 6-mercaptopurine after activation?
questions.why: Six-mercaptopurine metabolites inhibit pathways of de novo purine nucleotide production.

questions.stem: Which type of kinase converts a nucleoside monophosphate into a diphosphate?
questions.why: NMP kinases use an NTP phosphate donor to make an NDP.

questions.stem: Which carbon of the purine ring originates from bicarbonate during de novo synthesis?
questions.why: Carbon dioxide contributes carbon 6 of the purine ring.

questions.stem: Why is hydrolysis of pyrophosphate relevant to the committed purine biosynthetic step?

options.label: A
options.text: It supplies the ring carbon from glycine

options.label: B
options.text: It directly converts IMP into AMP

options.label: C
options.text: It helps drive the step forward

options.label: D
options.text: It releases ATP from the nucleotide

options.label: E
options.text: It allows uracil to bind PRPP

questions.why: Removal and hydrolysis of pyrophosphate favour formation of phosphoribosylamine and make the committed reaction effectively irreversible.

questions.stem: A drug reduces tetrahydrofolate availability. Why can it impede de novo purine synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: The ring is composed entirely of folate

options.label: B
options.text: Only PRPP synthetase depends on folate

options.label: E
options.text: Folate is the phosphate donor for AMP

questions.why: N10-formyl-THF contributes C2 and C8; antifolate drugs can interfere with de novo purine synthesis.

questions.stem: Pancreatic nucleases acting on ingested nucleic acids first generate which type of fragments?
questions.why: Dietary DNA and RNA are cut by nucleases into smaller oligonucleotides before further degradation.

questions.stem: A chemical inhibits orotidylate decarboxylase. Which compound would accumulate immediately upstream?
questions.why: Orotidine monophosphate is the direct substrate of the inhibited decarboxylase.

questions.stem: How many separate proteins contain the six key enzyme activities of mammalian de novo pyrimidine synthesis?
questions.why: The six activities are distributed across CAD, mitochondrial DHODH and bifunctional UMP synthase.

questions.stem: Which intermediate is formed just before the ribose-bearing nucleotide OMP appears?
questions.why: Dihydroorotate is oxidized to orotate, which next receives ribose phosphate from PRPP to yield OMP.

questions.stem: Which product from inosine phosphorolysis may be reused to regenerate ribose-5-phosphate?
questions.why: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase releases ribose-1-phosphate, which can be converted for re-use in PRPP synthesis.

questions.stem: Who demonstrated that immune serum could transfer diphtheria protection to another animal?
questions.why: The serum-transfer experiments provided early evidence of humoral immunity.

questions.stem: Which achievement is associated with Elie Metchnikoff?

options.label: D
options.text: Development of the first monoclonal antibody

questions.why: Metchnikoff observed cellular ingestion of foreign material and established a role for phagocytes in immunity.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes an adaptive response from an innate response?
questions.why: Adaptive immunity uses antigen-specific lymphocyte clones and generates memory.

questions.stem: Which protection is an example of naturally acquired passive immunity?

options.label: D
options.text: T cells primed by natural infection

questions.why: The infant receives ready-made maternal antibody without producing it itself.

questions.stem: Which organ is the primary maturation site for T lymphocytes?
questions.why: T cells undergo development and selection in the thymus.

questions.stem: Which organ is especially suited to surveying antigens circulating in the blood?
questions.why: The spleen filters blood and organizes immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

questions.stem: Naïve T lymphocytes commonly encounter antigen-bearing dendritic cells after those cells enter a:
questions.why: Dendritic cells migrate from tissues to lymph nodes, where naïve T cells are primed.

questions.stem: Which cell most commonly arrives early in an acute pyogenic bacterial infection?
questions.why: Neutrophils are rapidly recruited phagocytes in acute inflammation.

questions.stem: Which granulocyte is especially involved in defence against helminths?
questions.why: Eosinophils release toxic granule proteins during antihelminth responses.

questions.stem: Which tissue-resident cell is a major immediate source of histamine in allergy?
questions.why: Tissue mast cells degranulate in IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: A CD3-positive, CD8-positive lymphocyte is most likely which cell?
questions.why: CD3 identifies T cells and CD8 commonly identifies cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

questions.stem: Which marker is useful for identifying B lymphocytes in blood?
questions.why: CD19 is a characteristic B-lineage marker.

questions.stem: A lymphocyte is CD3-negative and CD16/CD56-positive. Which identity fits best?
questions.why: Typical NK cells express CD16/CD56 but lack CD3.

questions.stem: Which receptor permits NK cells to recognize IgG-coated targets during ADCC?
questions.why: NK-cell CD16 recognizes the Fc of bound IgG and triggers cytotoxicity.

questions.stem: Reduced MHC class I expression on a virus-infected cell favors NK-cell killing because it:

options.label: A
options.text: Improves antigen display to helper T cells

options.label: E
options.text: Blocks perforin release by NK cells

questions.why: NK inhibitory receptors normally detect self MHC I; loss of this signal makes targets more vulnerable.

questions.stem: Which effector pair is central to granule-mediated killing by NK cells?
questions.why: Perforin and granzymes act together to induce apoptosis of infected or malignant cells.

questions.stem: Which leukocyte surface antigen is especially associated with monocytes and macrophages?
questions.why: CD14 participates in microbial LPS recognition in the monocyte/macrophage lineage.

questions.stem: Which cell generally excels at presenting antigen to previously unprimed T lymphocytes?
questions.why: Dendritic cells express MHC and costimulatory molecules and are highly effective at priming naïve T cells.

questions.stem: How does innate immunity recognize microbes without rearranging antigen-receptor genes?

options.label: D
options.text: Clonal deletion of all tissue cells

options.label: E
options.text: Production of new TCRs in platelets

questions.why: Germline-encoded PRRs detect shared PAMPs on microbes.

questions.stem: Which receptor is chiefly associated with recognition of Gram-negative LPS?
questions.why: TLR4 recognizes LPS through an accessory receptor complex including MD-2 and CD14.

questions.stem: Which receptor detects bacterial flagellin?
questions.why: TLR5 is specialized for flagellin recognition.

questions.stem: Which receptor recognizes CpG-rich microbial DNA in endosomal vesicles?
questions.why: TLR9 recognizes unmethylated CpG motifs characteristic of many microbial DNA sequences.

questions.stem: NOD1 and NOD2 are particularly associated with detecting what in cells?
questions.why: NOD receptors recognize bacterial peptidoglycan-derived molecules in the cytosol.

questions.stem: The phagocyte respiratory burst begins with superoxide generation by which enzyme?
questions.why: NADPH oxidase reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide in activated phagocytes.

questions.stem: Which amino acid is the substrate for inducible nitric oxide synthase?
questions.why: iNOS produces nitric oxide and citrulline from arginine.

questions.stem: Which enzyme kills some bacteria by cleaving peptidoglycan bonds?
questions.why: Lysozyme degrades peptidoglycan, an oxygen-independent antimicrobial mechanism.

questions.stem: An immunogen differs from a non-immunogenic antigen because an immunogen can:

options.label: E
options.text: Cause immediate cell lysis without exposure

questions.why: Antigenicity is specific binding; immunogenicity includes the ability to induce an immune response.

questions.stem: A small drug molecule binds antibody but elicits little response until linked to a protein. The molecule is a:
questions.why: Haptens may bind specific antibodies but require carriers to become effective immunogens.

questions.stem: Which term describes the part of an antigen bound by an antibody?
questions.why: An epitope is an antigenic determinant, whereas the antibody's combining surface is the paratope.

questions.stem: What is the name of the antigen-binding region on an immunoglobulin?
questions.why: The paratope comprises variable-region residues that recognize a corresponding epitope.

questions.stem: Antibody binding lost when a native protein unfolds most strongly suggests recognition of a:
questions.why: Conformational determinants depend on the folded three-dimensional protein structure.

questions.stem: Conventional CD4 T cells chiefly recognize peptides displayed by which molecules?
questions.why: Extracellular antigens are generally presented by MHC II to CD4 T cells.

questions.stem: A nucleated cell presents cytosolic viral peptides to CD8 T cells using which molecules?
questions.why: MHC I presents endogenous peptides to CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

questions.stem: ABO blood-group differences between members of one species are examples of:
questions.why: Alloantigens differ between individuals of the same species.

questions.stem: A polysaccharide antigen stimulates B cells without T-helper contact. Which response is typical?

options.label: C
options.text: Direct recognition by peptide MHC I

questions.why: T-independent polysaccharides generally induce a limited-memory, largely IgM response.

questions.stem: What explains cross-reactivity between an antibody and two different antigens?
questions.why: Shared or structurally similar epitopes can permit recognition of more than one antigen.

questions.stem: What is the principal role of an adjuvant in a vaccine?
questions.why: Adjuvants enhance antigen presentation and innate activation to strengthen adaptive immune responses.

questions.stem: Bacterial superantigens can provoke systemic cytokine release by binding directly to:
questions.why: Superantigens bind MHC II and selected TCR Vβ regions outside the conventional antigen-binding groove, activating many T cells.

questions.stem: Which cell is primarily responsible for secreting large amounts of antigen-specific antibody?
questions.why: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B-lineage cells specialized for immunoglobulin secretion.

questions.stem: How many polypeptide chains form the basic immunoglobulin monomer?
questions.why: The basic antibody has two identical heavy and two identical light chains.

questions.stem: What determines whether an antibody is IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD or IgE?
questions.why: The heavy-chain constant domain defines the immunoglobulin class and associated effector properties.

questions.stem: Which two types of immunoglobulin light chains occur in humans?
questions.why: Each antibody uses either κ or λ light chains, not a mixture of both in one molecule.

questions.stem: Which portions of antibody heavy and light chains form the combining site?
questions.why: VH and VL domains together form the antigen-combining site.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of the antibody hinge region?
questions.why: The hinge allows Fab arms to adjust their orientation for binding antigens.

questions.stem: The hypervariable loops that most directly contact antigen are called:
questions.why: CDRs create much of the antibody-binding surface; framework segments structurally support them.

questions.stem: Which fragment of IgG retains antigen binding after papain digestion?
questions.why: Papain produces two monovalent Fab fragments and one Fc fragment.

questions.stem: Which fragment is typically produced by pepsin digestion of IgG and retains two binding sites?
questions.why: Pepsin generates bivalent F(ab′)2 while most of the Fc is degraded.

questions.stem: Which antibody region mediates binding to many Fc receptors and complement proteins?
questions.why: The constant Fc portion mediates many effector functions after antibody binding to antigen.

questions.stem: Which antibody class is transported across the human placenta to provide passive neonatal protection?
questions.why: IgG is transported by the neonatal Fc receptor and supplies maternal passive immunity.

questions.stem: Which class predominates in a primary antibody response before class switching?
questions.why: Naïve B-cell activation initially produces IgM; switching may generate other isotypes later.

questions.stem: Which structural form best describes secreted serum IgM?
questions.why: Secreted IgM is usually pentameric and is highly effective at complement activation and agglutination.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is predominant in mucosal secretions and colostrum?
questions.why: Dimeric secretory IgA protects mucosal surfaces against microbial attachment.

questions.stem: Which components are characteristic of secretory dimeric IgA?
questions.why: The J chain links IgA monomers; a secretory component aids transport and protects IgA in mucosal fluids.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is strongly linked to immediate allergy and helminth defence?
questions.why: IgE binds high-affinity Fcε receptors on mast cells and contributes to responses against parasitic worms.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is commonly expressed as an antigen receptor on mature naïve B cells?
questions.why: Mature naïve B cells typically coexpress membrane IgM and IgD.

questions.stem: A toxin is rendered unable to bind its host-cell receptor by a specific antibody. Which mechanism is illustrated?
questions.why: Antibody neutralization blocks the interaction of toxins or pathogens with host target cells.

questions.stem: Which term describes an antibody's overall multivalent binding strength?
questions.why: Avidity combines all binding interactions, whereas affinity describes one binding site–epitope interaction.

questions.stem: Which term describes strength between one epitope and one antibody combining site?
questions.why: Affinity is the intrinsic strength of a single antigen-binding interaction.

questions.stem: Which complement pathway is typically initiated when C1q binds antigen-bound IgG or IgM?
questions.why: The classical pathway is initiated by complement recognition of appropriate antibody–antigen complexes.

questions.stem: Which complement activation pathway is initiated by mannose-binding lectin on microbes?
questions.why: Mannose-binding lectin recognizes microbial carbohydrate patterns and activates MASP proteases.

questions.stem: Which complement pathway can amplify activation directly on susceptible microbial surfaces without specific antibody?
questions.why: The alternative pathway uses spontaneous C3 activation and surface amplification without antibody requirement.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment most directly promotes phagocytosis by coating microorganisms?
questions.why: C3b and its fragments act as opsonins recognized by complement receptors on phagocytes.

questions.stem: Which complement split product is a particularly powerful neutrophil chemoattractant?
questions.why: C5a is a major anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant that recruits and activates leukocytes.

questions.stem: Which complement components assemble into the membrane attack complex?
questions.why: Terminal complement components C5b–C9 generate pores in susceptible target membranes.

questions.stem: Which C3 convertase is formed by the classical and lectin complement pathways?
questions.why: The classical/lectin C3 convertase C4b2a cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b.

questions.stem: Which enzyme complex serves as the alternative-pathway C3 convertase?
questions.why: C3bBb is assembled from surface-bound C3b and factor B cleaved by factor D.

questions.stem: What is the predominant protective purpose of complement opsonization?

options.label: C
options.text: Converting all IgA molecules into IgG

options.label: E
options.text: Generating a fibrin clot without thrombin

questions.why: Complement fragments such as C3b coat pathogens and facilitate uptake by phagocytic complement receptors.

questions.stem: A deficiency in terminal complement components most directly impairs which function?

options.label: B
options.text: Processing of peptides for MHC II

options.label: C
options.text: Release of cytokines by plasma cells

questions.why: C5b–C9 forms the membrane attack complex; defects predispose particularly to Neisseria infections.

questions.stem: A cytokine acts on the same cell that secreted it. Which pattern of signalling is this?
questions.why: Autocrine cytokines act on the secreting cell via its own receptors.

questions.stem: A cytokine acts mainly on nearby cells in the tissue. Which pattern of signalling is illustrated?
questions.why: Paracrine signalling describes local action on neighbouring target cells.

questions.stem: One cytokine triggers different biological effects in several cell types. This property is called:
questions.why: Pleiotropy means a single cytokine has distinct activities on different target cells.

questions.stem: Two different cytokines stimulate the same biological effect. Which property is illustrated?
questions.why: Redundancy means distinct cytokines can share a function.

questions.stem: Two cytokines together produce a stronger effect than either alone. Their interaction is:
questions.why: Synergy describes cooperative enhancement of biological action.

questions.stem: Which chemokine is particularly associated with attracting neutrophils?
questions.why: CXCL8 is a neutrophil chemoattractant and participates in acute inflammation.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is important for T-cell proliferation after activation?
questions.why: Activated T cells produce IL-2 to support their proliferation and differentiation.

questions.stem: Which cytokine strongly activates macrophage microbicidal functions during Th1 responses?
questions.why: IFN-γ from Th1 and NK cells enhances macrophage activity against intracellular microbes.

questions.stem: Which pair is especially associated with early antiviral signalling by infected cells?
questions.why: Type I interferons induce antiviral responses in infected and nearby cells.

questions.stem: Severe infection causes macrophages to release cytokines linked to fever, capillary leakage and shock. Which pair is key?
questions.why: Excess TNF-α and IL-1 drive systemic inflammatory responses, vascular leakage and hypotension.

questions.stem: A defect in the common gamma-chain cytokine receptor can cause which condition?
questions.why: The shared IL-2Rγ chain is used by several cytokine receptors; defects cause X-linked SCID.

questions.stem: Defective IFN-γ receptor signalling particularly predisposes to infection with:
questions.why: IFN-γ is critical for macrophage activation in mycobacterial defence.

questions.stem: Which receptor-signalling mechanism is characteristic of many class I and II cytokine receptors?
questions.why: Many cytokine receptors recruit JAK kinases and STAT transcription factors to alter gene expression.

questions.stem: A biologic drug neutralizes TNF-α in rheumatoid arthritis. Which biological consequence is intended?
questions.why: Blocking TNF-α reduces a pro-inflammatory cytokine cascade implicated in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: Which immune mechanism is especially important during the earliest stages of many viral infections?
questions.why: IFN-α and IFN-β promote antiviral states in infected and nearby cells before full adaptive responses.

questions.stem: Which adaptive immune cell directly kills virus-infected cells displaying viral peptides on MHC class I?
questions.why: CD8 CTLs recognize viral peptide–MHC I and induce apoptosis through granzyme or Fas-mediated pathways.

questions.stem: For defence against extracellular pyogenic bacteria, which antibody function is particularly useful?
questions.why: Opsonizing IgG and complement mark bacteria for phagocyte ingestion.

questions.stem: Why are encapsulated bacteria sometimes difficult for phagocytes to clear?
questions.why: Polysaccharide capsules reduce phagocytosis; specific antibody helps overcome this defence.

questions.stem: Which secretory antibody helps prevent bacterial attachment to mucosal epithelium?
questions.why: Secretory IgA provides immune exclusion at mucosal surfaces.

questions.stem: Which response is particularly important against intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Direct action of platelet factor IV

questions.why: Th1-derived IFN-γ enhances macrophage microbicidal activity against intracellular mycobacteria.

questions.stem: A mutation produces a small progressive alteration in an influenza surface antigen. Which process is illustrated?
questions.why: Drift results from accumulated mutations that subtly change viral antigens.

questions.stem: A major reassortment of influenza genome segments creates a markedly new surface-antigen combination. This represents:
questions.why: Shift creates major antigenic changes through reassortment among influenza A strains.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is implicated in antibody-dependent enhancement during some dengue infections?

options.label: A
options.text: Fc receptor uptake of virus–IgG complexes

options.label: B
options.text: Destruction of MHC I by activated platelets

options.label: C
options.text: Prevention of virus binding by neutralizing IgA

options.label: D
options.text: Complement-mediated lysis of all infected cells

questions.why: Some non-neutralizing or cross-reactive antibodies facilitate infection of Fc-receptor-bearing cells.

questions.stem: A helminth infection triggers IgE production and eosinophil recruitment. Which helper T-cell pattern is most typical?
questions.why: Th2 cytokines favour IgE-associated immunity and eosinophil activity against helminths.

questions.stem: A protozoan lives mainly inside macrophages. Which protective response is most likely needed?
questions.why: Intracellular pathogens often require Th1 and macrophage-mediated immunity.

questions.stem: Which physical defence limits pathogen survival after entry into the stomach?
questions.why: Gastric acidity is a first-line non-specific barrier against ingested organisms.

questions.stem: Which inflammatory consequence is associated with high systemic TNF-α release in severe bacterial sepsis?
questions.why: Excess inflammatory cytokines promote vasodilation, increased permeability and circulatory shock.

questions.stem: A bacterial pathogen secretes an IgA protease. Which defence is most directly weakened?
questions.why: IgA proteases impair secretory IgA-dependent blockade of mucosal colonization.

questions.stem: Which immune pathway can explain kidney injury from deposition of circulating antigen–antibody complexes?
questions.why: Deposited immune complexes activate complement and recruit inflammatory cells, producing tissue injury.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between plasma and serum used for laboratory tests?
questions.why: Serum is the liquid after clotting and generally lacks fibrinogen; plasma comes from anticoagulated blood.

questions.stem: What does an antibody titre report in a serial dilution test?

options.label: C
options.text: Total mass of albumin in the sample

options.label: D
options.text: Amount of free complement in plasma

questions.why: Titre is the highest dilution at which a defined antigen–antibody reaction remains detectable.

questions.stem: A highly sensitive assay is particularly useful because it tends to minimize:
questions.why: Sensitivity is the proportion of truly affected individuals who test positive.

questions.stem: A highly specific diagnostic assay is particularly useful because it tends to minimize:
questions.why: Specificity is the proportion of unaffected individuals who test negative.

questions.stem: Why can undiluted serum with extremely high antibody concentration give a falsely weak precipitation reaction?
questions.why: The prozone effect occurs when antibody excess limits lattice formation; dilution can restore the visible reaction.

questions.stem: A precipitin reaction is weak because the specimen contains far more antigen than antibody. This condition is:
questions.why: Antigen excess may prevent extensive lattice formation in a precipitation assay.

questions.stem: Maximum visible precipitation of soluble antigen and antibody usually occurs in which region?
questions.why: At equivalence, multivalent antigen and antibodies form large cross-linked lattices.

questions.stem: Which reaction is most appropriate for visibly clumping antibody-coated particulate cells?
questions.why: Agglutination forms visible aggregates of particulate antigens or cells.

questions.stem: Which technique relies on an enzyme-linked reagent to produce a measurable colour signal?
questions.why: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays use an enzyme reporter and chromogenic or other detectable substrate.

questions.stem: Which assay directly uses a radionuclide label as part of its detection system?
questions.why: Radioimmunoassays use radiolabelled tracers to measure antigen–antibody reactions.

questions.stem: What best distinguishes avidity from affinity in antibody–antigen binding?
questions.why: Avidity integrates multivalent interactions; affinity concerns one epitope–paratope contact.

questions.stem: Antibodies against a related species produce a positive serological result. Which limitation best explains it?
questions.why: Cross-reactivity can cause false-positive serology when related antigens have similar determinants.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes active immunity obtained by routine vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Preformed antibody is supplied from a donor

options.label: B
options.text: The host is protected only by innate barriers

options.label: C
options.text: Protective antibodies arise from donor plasma

options.label: D
options.text: Host lymphocytes produce the protective response

options.label: E
options.text: The vaccine directly digests circulating microbes

questions.why: Active immunization stimulates host B- and T-cell responses and can generate memory.

questions.stem: Which component of a vaccine primarily supplies the specificity of the immune response?
questions.why: The antigen is recognized by adaptive immunity and determines the specificity of the response.

questions.stem: Which vaccine component is included chiefly to enhance immunogenicity?
questions.why: Adjuvants improve immune activation and can enhance the resulting adaptive response.

questions.stem: Which vaccine component is included chiefly to reduce microbial contamination of multi-dose preparations?
questions.why: Preservatives inhibit unintended microbial growth during storage and use of certain vaccine formulations.

questions.stem: Why is a toxoid vaccine able to produce protection without causing the toxin's disease?

options.label: E
options.text: It blocks all host antibody responses

questions.why: Toxoids are inactivated toxins that preserve antigenic structures capable of inducing neutralizing antibody.

questions.stem: What is the key aim of linking a bacterial polysaccharide to a carrier protein in a conjugate vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: Suppress antigen uptake by dendritic cells

options.label: B
options.text: Prevent formation of memory B cells

options.label: D
options.text: Recruit T-cell help for the B-cell response

options.label: E
options.text: Directly kill bacteria in the syringe

questions.why: Conjugation recruits T-dependent help, supporting improved class switching and memory.

questions.stem: Which vaccine type contains a weakened organism capable of limited replication in the host?
questions.why: Live attenuated organisms replicate to a limited extent and can induce strong adaptive immunity.

questions.stem: What is the primary immunological purpose of a booster dose?

options.label: A
options.text: Replace every host innate immune cell

options.label: E
options.text: Eliminate all existing memory T cells

questions.why: Boosters recall memory clones and generally increase the magnitude and durability of immune responses.

questions.stem: Which mechanism defines a classic type I hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: Type I hypersensitivity follows sensitization and IgE cross-linking on mast cells during re-exposure.

questions.stem: Which molecule is the principal preformed mediator released rapidly by degranulating mast cells?
questions.why: Histamine is stored in mast-cell granules and causes vasodilation, permeability and bronchoconstrictor effects.

questions.stem: Which class of hypersensitivity best describes antibody-mediated destruction of transfused red cells?
questions.why: Type II involves IgG or IgM directed against cell-surface or extracellular-matrix antigens.

questions.stem: Which class of hypersensitivity is characterized by deposition of soluble antigen–antibody complexes?
questions.why: Type III immune complexes can lodge in vessels or glomeruli and activate complement.

questions.stem: Which mechanism underlies allergic contact dermatitis from a sensitizing chemical?
questions.why: Contact dermatitis is typically a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells.

questions.stem: A tuberculin skin test becomes indurated after roughly 48–72 hours. This is an example of:
questions.why: Delayed-type hypersensitivity is driven by antigen-specific T cells and recruited macrophages.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes type II from type III hypersensitivity?

options.label: A
options.text: Type II is driven by IgE while type III uses T cells

options.label: B
options.text: Antibody binds fixed rather than soluble targets

options.label: C
options.text: Type II occurs only in the respiratory epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: Type III requires perforin release by CD8 cells

options.label: E
options.text: Type III has no antibody contribution

questions.why: Type II usually involves antibody against fixed cellular or matrix targets; type III involves deposited soluble immune complexes.

questions.stem: A second allergen exposure cross-links mast-cell-bound IgE. Which event is expected immediately?
questions.why: Cross-linking FcεRI-bound IgE triggers mast-cell mediator release during immediate hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: Which cell contributes prominently to many late-phase allergic reactions?
questions.why: Th2 cytokines recruit eosinophils, which contribute to later tissue inflammation.

questions.stem: Which retinal photoreceptors are especially adapted for dim-light vision?
questions.why: Rods are more light-sensitive and mediate scotopic, mainly monochromatic vision.

questions.stem: Which photoreceptors are principally responsible for colour vision in bright light?
questions.why: Cones mediate photopic vision and have different opsins underlying colour discrimination.

questions.stem: Which property makes rods more sensitive than cones in dim light?

options.label: C
options.text: Higher acuity at the foveal centre

options.label: E
options.text: Direct excitation of optic nerve axons

questions.why: Rods respond to low photon intensities, whereas cones require brighter illumination.

questions.stem: Rhodopsin consists of the apoprotein opsin combined with which light-sensitive molecule?
questions.why: The chromophore of dark-adapted rhodopsin is 11-cis-retinal derived from vitamin A.

questions.stem: Which vitamin is the nutritional precursor of the retinal chromophore?
questions.why: Vitamin A supplies retinoids, including retinal required for visual pigment regeneration.

questions.stem: Which symptom is a classic early functional consequence of vitamin A deficiency?
questions.why: Inadequate vitamin A impairs rhodopsin regeneration and causes poor vision in dim light.

questions.stem: Which dietary compound is a provitamin A source from plant foods?
questions.why: Beta-carotene is a carotenoid that can be cleaved to supply vitamin A.

questions.stem: Which visual-pigment component differs among the three principal cone classes?
questions.why: Cone pigments share the 11-cis-retinal chromophore; differences in opsin tune their absorption spectra.

questions.stem: Which molecular change is initiated when a photon is absorbed by rhodopsin?
questions.why: Light rapidly isomerizes the chromophore from 11-cis to all-trans, triggering opsin activation.

questions.stem: Which form of rhodopsin is the principal active G-protein-signalling state after illumination?
questions.why: Activated rhodopsin (metarhodopsin II) catalyses activation of transducin.

questions.stem: What is the immediate nucleotide-exchange event in transducin activation?

options.label: C
options.text: GTP is converted to cyclic GMP

questions.why: Activated rhodopsin promotes GDP release and GTP binding on the transducin alpha subunit.

questions.stem: The alpha subunit of activated transducin acts primarily on which effector enzyme?
questions.why: GTP-bound transducin activates PDE6, which hydrolyses cGMP.

questions.stem: What happens to cytoplasmic cGMP in a rod after rhodopsin activates transducin?
questions.why: PDE hydrolyses cGMP, lowering free cGMP in the outer segment.

questions.stem: In a rod outer segment, decreased cGMP chiefly causes which channel response?
questions.why: Reduced cGMP closes cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels, diminishing Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ entry.

questions.stem: What is the change in a rod photoreceptor's membrane potential when light activates phototransduction?
questions.why: Light closes the dark-current cation channels, making rods more negative.

questions.stem: Why is a rod relatively depolarized in darkness?

options.label: E
options.text: All retinal is maintained in the trans form

questions.why: In darkness, high cGMP keeps channels open, permitting inward dark current.

questions.stem: Which intracellular ionic concentration typically falls after illumination of a rod?
questions.why: Light closes Ca²⁺-permeable channels while extrusion continues, lowering free calcium.

questions.stem: A rod is exposed to light. Which change in synaptic transmitter release is expected?
questions.why: Rod hyperpolarization reduces tonic glutamate secretion at its synapse.

questions.stem: Which enzyme adds phosphate groups to activated rhodopsin to begin its shutoff?
questions.why: Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates activated rhodopsin at C-terminal serine/threonine residues.

questions.stem: Which protein blocks further transducin activation by binding phosphorylated rhodopsin?
questions.why: Arrestin binds phosphorylated activated rhodopsin and prevents additional G-protein coupling.

questions.stem: How is activated transducin alpha switched off during recovery from a flash?

options.label: A
options.text: Hydrolysis of bound GTP to GDP

options.label: E
options.text: Formation of ATP from free AMP

questions.why: Intrinsic GTPase activity returns transducin alpha to the GDP-bound inactive state.

questions.stem: After a light flash, how is cGMP restored to reopen photoreceptor cation channels?
questions.why: Guanylate cyclase replenishes cGMP, supporting channel reopening.

questions.stem: The light-induced reduction in rod calcium helps recovery partly by promoting which effect?
questions.why: Lower Ca²⁺ stimulates guanylate cyclase through calcium-sensitive regulatory proteins.

questions.stem: Why does photoreceptor calcium continue to decline briefly after light closes outer-segment channels?

options.label: B
options.text: Calcium is irreversibly bound to rhodopsin

options.label: D
options.text: Transducin pumps calcium into the lens

options.label: E
options.text: Calcium efflux persists as influx falls

questions.why: A Na⁺/Ca²⁺,K⁺ exchanger continues to extrude Ca²⁺ after channel-mediated entry diminishes.

questions.stem: Which event most directly helps prevent an activated rhodopsin molecule from repeatedly activating transducin?

options.label: A
options.text: Retinal attachment to free vitamin D

questions.why: Kinase phosphorylation followed by arrestin binding terminates continued rhodopsin signalling.

questions.stem: Recovery from bleaching requires returning retinal into which configuration for rhodopsin regeneration?
questions.why: All-trans-retinoids are processed in the retinoid cycle to regenerate 11-cis-retinal.

questions.stem: After moving from bright sunlight into a dark room, rod sensitivity improves over time. This is called:
questions.why: Dark adaptation includes pigment regeneration and neural adjustments that increase visual sensitivity.

questions.stem: Which adaptation is occurring when the visual system reduces sensitivity during prolonged bright illumination?
questions.why: Light adaptation limits saturation and helps vision function across large changes in illumination.

questions.stem: What is the main biochemical purpose of the visual retinoid cycle?

options.label: C
options.text: Conversion of opsin into rhodopsin kinase

questions.why: The retinoid cycle converts bleached all-trans chromophore back to the 11-cis form for pigment regeneration.

questions.stem: The three functional cone pigment classes differ mainly in which property?

options.label: B
options.text: Presence of a different vitamin A

questions.why: Different opsin environments shift the wavelengths at which cone pigments absorb most strongly.

questions.stem: A patient cannot distinguish many reds and greens because one cone pigment is abnormal. Which mechanism fits?

options.label: B
options.text: A deficiency in rod rhodopsin kinase

options.label: E
options.text: Complete loss of all optic nerve axons

questions.why: Red–green colour vision defects commonly arise from X-linked cone opsin gene changes.

questions.stem: Why is red–green colour deficiency more common in males?
questions.why: The red- and green-sensitive cone opsin genes are located on the X chromosome.

questions.stem: If the three cone pigments contain the same chromophore, why do they absorb different wavelengths?

options.label: A
options.text: Each contains a different retinal isomer

options.label: C
options.text: Each cone uses a different metal cofactor

options.label: D
options.text: All cones contain distinct vitamin molecules

questions.why: A shared 11-cis-retinal chromophore is spectrally tuned by different opsin amino-acid environments.

questions.stem: After light exposure, which combination correctly summarizes the initial rod response?
questions.why: Activated transducin stimulates PDE6, lowering cGMP and closing cation channels.

questions.stem: A defect prevents transducin from exchanging GDP for GTP. Which result is most likely immediately after illumination?
questions.why: GTP loading activates transducin so it can stimulate PDE; failure blunts the light response.

questions.stem: Which protein family provides the major tensile strength of many connective tissues?
questions.why: Collagen fibrils are major load-bearing elements of skin, tendon, bone and many other tissues.

questions.stem: What is the principal supramolecular structure of a collagen tropocollagen molecule?
questions.why: Tropocollagen contains three alpha chains arranged into an elongated triple helix.

questions.stem: Which amino acid occupies approximately every third position in the collagen triple helix?
questions.why: Glycine's small side chain permits close packing toward the helix axis.

questions.stem: Which repeating primary-sequence pattern is characteristic of collagen?
questions.why: Collagen has a Gly-X-Y repeat, commonly with proline and hydroxyproline at X/Y positions.

questions.stem: Why is glycine replacement within a collagen alpha chain frequently damaging?

options.label: A
options.text: It prevents all peptide bond formation

questions.why: Only glycine is small enough for the crowded inner helix; substitutions can destabilize assembly.

questions.stem: Which collagen type is especially abundant in bone, skin and tendon?
questions.why: Type I forms thick tensile fibrils in bone, skin, tendon and ligaments.

questions.stem: Which collagen type is the main fibrillar collagen of hyaline cartilage?
questions.why: Type II collagen is characteristic of cartilage and contributes to its fibrillar framework.

questions.stem: Which collagen type is most closely associated with reticular fibres in vessels and internal organs?
questions.why: Type III forms reticular fibrils and occurs in vessels, skin and internal organs.

questions.stem: Which collagen type organizes into sheet-like networks in basement membranes?
questions.why: Type IV forms network-like scaffolds of the basal lamina rather than typical long fibrils.

questions.stem: Anchoring fibrils beneath stratified squamous epithelia contain mainly which collagen type?
questions.why: Type VII collagen forms anchoring fibrils that help attach the basement membrane to underlying connective tissue.

questions.stem: In which cellular compartment does translation of collagen precursor chains begin?
questions.why: Preprocollagen chains enter the rough ER during translation for modification and assembly.

questions.stem: Which reaction generates hydroxyproline residues during collagen processing?
questions.why: Prolyl hydroxylase acts on selected proline residues already incorporated into procollagen chains.

questions.stem: Which nutrient is needed to keep iron available in the reduced state for collagen prolyl hydroxylase?
questions.why: Ascorbate maintains iron in the Fe²⁺ state required for efficient collagen hydroxylation.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly lists key requirements for collagen prolyl hydroxylation?
questions.why: Prolyl hydroxylase is an Fe²⁺-dependent dioxygenase using oxygen and alpha-ketoglutarate; ascorbate maintains Fe²⁺.

questions.stem: The hydroxylation of certain collagen lysine residues is carried out by which enzyme?
questions.why: Lysyl hydroxylase acts intracellularly on lysine residues prior to full triple-helix assembly.

questions.stem: Which modified collagen amino acid is a major site of subsequent carbohydrate addition?
questions.why: Galactose and sometimes glucose are linked to selected hydroxylysine residues.

questions.stem: Which pair of sugars can be sequentially attached to hydroxylysine residues?
questions.why: Nascent collagen can be glycosylated on hydroxylysine with galactosyl and glucosyl residues.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of hydroxyproline on the collagen triple helix?
questions.why: Proline hydroxylation stabilizes collagen's triple helix near physiological temperature.

questions.stem: What prevents intracellular procollagen from prematurely aggregating into mature extracellular fibrils?
questions.why: N- and C-terminal propeptides keep procollagen soluble before extracellular processing.

questions.stem: Where are the terminal procollagen propeptides ordinarily removed before fibril assembly?
questions.why: Extracellular procollagen peptidases remove terminal peptides to form tropocollagen.

questions.stem: Which process most directly converts procollagen into tropocollagen after secretion?
questions.why: Procollagen proteinases cleave terminal propeptides outside cells, allowing fibril self-assembly.

questions.stem: Which enzyme initiates oxidative cross-linking by converting selected collagen lysines into aldehydes?
questions.why: Lysyl oxidase oxidatively deaminates lysine/hydroxylysine residues, producing reactive aldehydes for cross-links.

questions.stem: Which modified residue forms when lysyl oxidase oxidatively deaminates lysine in collagen?
questions.why: Allysine is an aldehyde-bearing derivative of lysine involved in covalent collagen cross-links.

questions.stem: Which cofactor metal is associated with lysyl oxidase-mediated cross-link formation?
questions.why: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent amine oxidase required for collagen and elastin cross-linking.

questions.stem: What is the principal mechanical benefit of intermolecular collagen cross-links?
questions.why: Covalent cross-links strengthen mature fibrils and provide resistance to mechanical pulling.

questions.stem: Which disorder results when vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen proline hydroxylation?
questions.why: Scurvy lowers collagen stability, causing weak capillaries, gingival bleeding and impaired wound healing.

questions.stem: Bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhage and impaired wound healing most strongly suggest deficiency of:
questions.why: Vitamin C deficiency causes defective collagen hydroxylation and fragile connective tissues.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes scurvy from a primary clotting-factor deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of the coagulation factor VIII gene

options.label: D
options.text: Weak collagen makes vessel walls fragile

questions.why: Scurvy produces vascular fragility due to collagen defects, even without a primary coagulation factor defect.

questions.stem: A child has frequent fractures and a mutation involving type I collagen. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.why: Type I collagen defects can compromise bone matrix and produce brittle bones.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern strongly suggests an Ehlers–Danlos syndrome?
questions.why: EDS comprises heritable connective-tissue disorders with variable skin fragility and joint hypermobility.

questions.stem: Some forms of Ehlers–Danlos syndrome arise from defective processing by which enzyme?
questions.why: Impaired extracellular removal of procollagen propeptides can disrupt fibrillogenesis.

questions.stem: A plant toxin inhibits lysyl oxidase and produces collagen with poor cross-linking. This is characteristic of:
questions.why: Beta-aminopropionitrile associated with lathyrism inhibits lysyl oxidase-mediated cross-linking.

questions.stem: Which extracellular protein is chiefly responsible for reversible stretch in elastic fibres?
questions.why: Elastin networks provide elastic recoil, contrasting with collagen's tensile rigidity.

questions.stem: Which amino-acid composition best distinguishes mature elastin from collagen?
questions.why: Unlike collagen, elastin contains very little hydroxyproline, no hydroxylysine, and many nonpolar residues.

questions.stem: Which distinctive elastic-fibre cross-link is derived from four lysine residues?
questions.why: Desmosine cross-links derive from four lysine side chains and are characteristic of mature elastin.

questions.stem: Why do mature elastin fibres recoil after stretching?

options.label: B
options.text: Complete hydrolysis of elastic peptide bonds

options.label: D
options.text: Continuous formation of new fibrin fibres

questions.why: Lysine-derived cross-links connect mobile elastin chains, allowing extensibility and elastic recoil.

questions.stem: Which cell is a major producer of collagen during connective-tissue repair?
questions.why: Fibroblasts produce extracellular collagen and other matrix proteins during wound healing.

questions.stem: During scar maturation, which change most directly contributes to increasing tensile strength?

options.label: C
options.text: Degradation of all type I collagen

questions.why: Remodelling includes increased collagen organization and covalent cross-linking.

questions.stem: Which fibroblast-related cell type provides contractile force during wound contraction?
questions.why: Myofibroblasts express contractile proteins and help shrink healing wounds.

questions.stem: A hormone circulates widely but alters only certain cells. Which property chiefly explains this selectivity?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher plasma viscosity in target tissues

options.label: B
options.text: Greater red-cell number near target cells

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of a matching cellular receptor

options.label: D
options.text: Higher calcium concentration in every cell

options.label: E
options.text: Absence of hepatic blood flow to targets

questions.why: Hormonal target specificity depends primarily on whether responsive cells express the appropriate receptors.

questions.stem: Besides hormone concentration, which two factors influence the degree of target-cell activation?

options.label: C
options.text: Tissue collagen type and fibre length

questions.why: Responses depend on circulating hormone, receptor number and hormone–receptor affinity.

questions.stem: Why can adipose tissue be considered an endocrine organ?

options.label: B
options.text: It secretes digestive enzymes into ducts

questions.why: Adipose tissue releases endocrine mediators affecting energy homeostasis and inflammatory signalling.

questions.stem: Which organ has both an endocrine function and a separate exocrine function?
questions.why: Islets secrete hormones into blood, while pancreatic acini produce digestive secretions into ducts.

questions.stem: Which hormone is chemically a glycoprotein hormone?
questions.why: TSH is a glycoprotein, as are FSH and LH.

questions.stem: Which hormone is derived primarily from cholesterol?
questions.why: Cortisol is a steroid hormone synthesized from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex.

questions.stem: Which hormone is derived from an amino acid but acts predominantly via an intracellular receptor?
questions.why: Thyroid hormones are tyrosine-derived but bind nuclear thyroid hormone receptors to regulate transcription.

questions.stem: Which pair consists of peptide or protein hormones?
questions.why: Insulin and glucagon are peptide hormones, unlike steroids and amino acid derivatives.

questions.stem: Which class of hormones is generally hydrophobic and crosses cell membranes to bind intracellular receptors?
questions.why: Steroid hormones diffuse across lipid membranes and regulate gene expression through intracellular receptors.

questions.stem: Which hormone is a catecholamine derived from tyrosine?
questions.why: Epinephrine is a tyrosine-derived catecholamine acting largely through cell-surface adrenergic receptors.

questions.stem: Activation of a Gs-coupled hormone receptor most directly stimulates which enzyme?
questions.why: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cAMP.

questions.stem: Which molecule serves as the immediate precursor of cAMP in hormonal signalling?
questions.why: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into the second messenger cyclic AMP.

questions.stem: What is a principal intracellular target of cyclic AMP?
questions.why: cAMP activates PKA, leading to phosphorylation-dependent cellular responses.

questions.stem: How does the G protein act when a surface hormone receptor is activated?

options.label: A
options.text: ATP is converted into DNA directly

options.label: B
options.text: GTP is converted into cyclic AMP directly

options.label: D
options.text: The alpha subunit exchanges GDP for GTP

options.label: E
options.text: The receptor synthesizes cAMP from GTP

questions.why: Receptor activation promotes GDP–GTP exchange on the G-protein alpha subunit.

questions.stem: Which enzyme cleaves PIP2 during Gq-coupled receptor signalling?
questions.why: Gq activates phospholipase C, producing IP3 and DAG from PIP2.

questions.stem: Which two second messengers are generated from PIP2?
questions.why: Phospholipase C hydrolyses PIP2 into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol.

questions.stem: Which messenger directly triggers calcium release from endoplasmic reticulum stores?
questions.why: IP3 binds IP3 receptors on intracellular stores and releases Ca²⁺.

questions.stem: Which downstream effector is classically activated by diacylglycerol?
questions.why: DAG activates PKC, often with calcium contributions, to phosphorylate target proteins.

questions.stem: Which calcium-binding protein mediates many intracellular effects of increased Ca²⁺?
questions.why: Calmodulin binds Ca²⁺ and regulates diverse enzymes and cellular functions.

questions.stem: Which mechanism terminates cAMP signals by hydrolysing cyclic AMP?
questions.why: Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases convert cAMP into noncyclic AMP.

questions.stem: Which hormone below signals principally through a receptor tyrosine kinase rather than a G-protein receptor?
questions.why: The insulin receptor has intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, an important exception to a blanket peptide–GPCR rule.

questions.stem: Which hormone acts through a receptor linked to JAK–STAT rather than intrinsic receptor tyrosine kinase activity?
questions.why: Growth hormone uses cytokine-like receptors associated with JAK2 and downstream STAT transcription factors.

questions.stem: Which event is most directly triggered when an activated steroid-receptor complex binds regulatory DNA?

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate opening of all sodium channels

options.label: D
options.text: Conversion of ATP into cyclic GMP

questions.why: Steroid receptors act as ligand-dependent transcription regulators.

questions.stem: Why are classical genomic steroid effects often slower to appear than many peptide-hormone effects?

options.label: A
options.text: They require release of preformed histamine

options.label: C
options.text: They depend on a membrane GTPase only

options.label: D
options.text: They require synthesis of new proteins

options.label: E
options.text: They directly open epithelial ion channels

questions.why: Classical steroid responses involve transcription and subsequent synthesis of proteins.

questions.stem: What is the common starting substrate for synthesis of adrenal corticosteroids?
questions.why: Both adrenal glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids derive from cholesterol.

questions.stem: The first common steroidogenic product formed from cholesterol in the mitochondrion is:
questions.why: Cholesterol side-chain cleavage yields pregnenolone, the common steroid precursor.

questions.stem: Which adrenal cortical zone synthesizes aldosterone most directly?
questions.why: The zona glomerulosa produces mineralocorticoids and lacks significant 17α-hydroxylase activity.

questions.stem: Which steroidogenic enzyme activity is characteristically absent from the zona glomerulosa?
questions.why: The zona glomerulosa does not express CYP17A1 and thus does not follow cortisol/androgen pathways.

questions.stem: What is the major glucocorticoid normally produced by the human adrenal cortex?
questions.why: Cortisol is the predominant glucocorticoid in humans.

questions.stem: Which endocrine effect is most characteristic of aldosterone?
questions.why: Aldosterone stimulates distal nephron sodium reabsorption and usually promotes potassium secretion.

questions.stem: Which metabolic effect is consistent with cortisol action during stress?
questions.why: Cortisol increases gluconeogenic capacity and mobilizes substrates during stress.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly represents the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis?
questions.why: Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary ACTH, which stimulates adrenal cortisol production.

questions.stem: What is the effect of increased cortisol on hypothalamic CRH and anterior-pituitary ACTH?

options.label: D
options.text: Direct conversion of ACTH into cortisol

questions.stem: What distinguishes somatic from germline gene therapy?

options.label: A
options.text: Somatic changes are not normally inherited

options.label: C
options.text: Somatic treatment requires no delivery vector

options.label: D
options.text: Germline treatment affects only skin cells

questions.why: Somatic therapy targets non-reproductive cells; germline changes could be passed to offspring.

questions.stem: Why are retroviral vectors used cautiously in integrating gene therapy?

options.label: A
options.text: Their genomes cannot enter mammalian cells

options.label: C
options.text: Insertion may disrupt or activate host genes

options.label: D
options.text: They lack any nucleic acid cargo

options.label: E
options.text: They never produce stable gene expression

questions.why: Integration creates a risk of insertional mutagenesis, including proto-oncogene activation.

questions.stem: Which biotechnological application best illustrates manufacturing a therapeutic protein using engineered microbes?

options.label: A
options.text: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

questions.why: Recombinant insulin is produced by expressing human insulin sequences in engineered production hosts.

questions.stem: What is a principal challenge in ex vivo gene transfer to patient cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of RNA inside all human cells

options.label: E
options.text: Inability to culture any human cells

questions.why: Gene therapy must achieve sufficient corrected-cell numbers without unsafe integration or expression.

questions.stem: Which test strategy detects a known single-base mutation by sequence-specific probe hybridization?
questions.why: An allele-specific oligonucleotide can distinguish a normal from a mutant sequence under controlled hybridization.

questions.stem: What is the principal role of a radiolabelled or fluorescent DNA probe in molecular diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Catalyse DNA synthesis on its own

questions.why: Probes detect matching DNA or RNA sequences through complementary base pairing.

questions.stem: Which feature is particularly useful when selecting a DNA cloning vector for downstream protein expression?

options.label: E
options.text: Inability to replicate inside host cells

questions.why: Successful expression requires transcriptional and translational regulatory elements that function in the chosen host.

questions.stem: Which enzyme deficiency causes the classic Lesch–Nyhan syndrome?
questions.why: HGPRT deficiency impairs purine salvage, increasing PRPP-driven synthesis and uric acid formation.

questions.stem: A child with excessive urate production, neurological abnormalities and self-injurious behaviour most likely has:
questions.why: Severe HGPRT deficiency causes the classic neurological and hyperuricaemic features of Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.

questions.stem: Why does severe adenosine deaminase deficiency damage lymphocyte development?

options.label: E
options.text: Increased catabolism of uracil into beta-alanine

questions.why: ADA deficiency causes toxic deoxyadenosine/dATP accumulation and can cause severe combined immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A patient with ADA deficiency has severe recurrent infections in infancy. Which immune diagnosis is most consistent?
questions.why: ADA deficiency can result in marked T- and B-cell dysfunction, producing SCID.

questions.stem: Which drug reduces uric acid production by inhibiting xanthine oxidase?
questions.why: Allopurinol is converted to oxypurinol, a xanthine oxidoreductase inhibitor used for lowering urate.

questions.stem: What is the immediate effect of xanthine oxidase inhibition on purine degradation?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased conversion of guanine into GMP

options.label: B
options.text: Increased salvage of thymine to TMP

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced degradation of uracil to beta-alanine

options.label: E
options.text: Reduced conversion of xanthine to urate

questions.why: Xanthine oxidase catalyses the terminal steps toward uric acid; inhibition decreases urate synthesis.

questions.stem: Why can excessive PRPP availability favour hyperuricaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: It destroys renal urate transporters directly

options.label: B
options.text: It drives increased de novo purine synthesis

options.label: C
options.text: It prevents formation of all pyrimidines

options.label: D
options.text: It converts uric acid back into inosine

options.label: E
options.text: It blocks the xanthine oxidase reaction

questions.why: High PRPP supports increased purine synthesis and eventually increased purine degradation to urate.

questions.stem: Which inflammatory deposit is characteristic of acute gout?
questions.why: Hyperuricaemia promotes monosodium urate deposition, typically causing painful synovial inflammation.

questions.stem: Why can hypoxanthine–guanine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency increase purine de novo synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Less salvage leaves more PRPP available

options.label: B
options.text: It directly synthesizes more xanthine oxidase

options.label: C
options.text: It stimulates DNA ligase to make purines

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents all ribose phosphate formation

options.label: E
options.text: It decreases glutamine supply to the liver

questions.why: With failed salvage, PRPP accumulates and inhibitory nucleotide pools fall, encouraging de novo synthesis.

questions.stem: Which metabolic result explains the neurological and immune phenotype of severe ADA deficiency?

options.label: B
options.text: Excess ornithine blocks the urea cycle

questions.why: Raised dATP disrupts ribonucleotide reductase activity and DNA precursor homeostasis, especially in lymphocytes.

questions.stem: 6-Mercaptopurine must undergo which reaction to form active nucleotide analogues in cells?
questions.why: HGPRT salvages 6-mercaptopurine with PRPP to form thio-IMP, which interferes with purine synthesis.

questions.stem: Which distinction between mammalian CPS I and CPS II is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: CPS I is cytosolic; CPS II is mitochondrial

options.label: B
options.text: CPS I is mitochondrial; CPS II is cytosolic

options.label: C
options.text: Both enzymes function only in the nucleus

options.label: D
options.text: Both enzymes use only free ammonia

options.label: E
options.text: CPS II functions in the urea cycle

questions.why: CPS I initiates mitochondrial urea synthesis using ammonia; CPS II initiates cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis using glutamine.
